script.title: Numerische Methoden (lecture notes)
script.note: Page numbers are PDF pages; the printed page number is one less.

exam.format: Part 1: multiple choice, marked (S) single-correct or (M) multiple-correct, often 'which statement is wrong'. Part 2: open questions with derivations, error/convergence analysis and code completion (Python/numpy in this course).

chapters.title: Before the start: rounding, cost, matrices

concepts.title: Vector spaces, bases and coordinates
concepts.summary: A basis lets you write every vector uniquely as a linear combination of basis vectors; the coefficients are its coordinates.
concepts.why: Interpolation and Fourier methods are all 'pick a basis, find the coordinates'.

concepts.title: Inner products, norms and orthogonality
concepts.summary: An inner product ⟨u,v⟩ measures alignment, induces the norm ‖v‖ = √⟨v,v⟩, and u ⟂ v means ⟨u,v⟩ = 0. The same idea works for functions with integrals.
concepts.why: Fourier coefficients, Chebyshev orthogonality and least squares are all projections defined by an inner product.

concepts.title: Orthonormal bases and change of basis
concepts.summary: In an orthonormal basis the coordinates are simply inner products c_k = ⟨v,q_k⟩, and the basis matrix Q satisfies Q⁻¹ = Qᴴ.
concepts.why: This is exactly why the DFT is cheap to invert and why QR is stable.

concepts.title: Complex numbers and Euler's formula
concepts.summary: e^{iθ} = cos θ + i sin θ turns rotations into multiplication: |e^{iθ}| = 1 and e^{iθ}e^{iφ} = e^{i(θ+φ)}.
concepts.why: Trigonometric interpolation and the DFT are written entirely in complex exponentials.

concepts.title: Taylor expansion and remainder
concepts.summary: f(x+h) = f(x) + h f'(x) + … + hⁿ f⁽ⁿ⁾(x)/n! + O(hⁿ⁺¹); the remainder tells you how an error scales with h.
concepts.why: Error orders of difference quotients, quadrature rules and Newton's method all come from Taylor.

concepts.title: Floating-point numbers and rounding errors
concepts.summary: Doubles carry a relative precision of about ε ≈ 2.2·10⁻¹⁶; every operation adds a relative error of that size, and very small or large numbers under- or overflow.
concepts.why: Every later accuracy statement is bounded below by these errors.

concepts.title: Cancellation and stable reformulation
concepts.summary: Subtracting two nearly equal numbers keeps their absolute error but destroys the relative accuracy; rewriting the formula (e.g. for the roots of a quadratic) avoids it.
concepts.why: It explains why naive formulas like (f(x+h) − f(x))/h fail for tiny h.

concepts.title: Complex-step derivative
concepts.summary: f'(x) ≈ Im f(x+ih)/h involves no subtraction, so h can be tiny and the result is accurate to machine precision.
concepts.why: A neat example of designing a formula around cancellation.

concepts.title: Richardson extrapolation
concepts.summary: If an approximation has an error expansion c·hᵖ + …, combining the results for h and h/2 cancels the leading term and raises the order.
concepts.why: The same trick powers Romberg integration in chapter 5.

concepts.title: Computational cost and asymptotic complexity
concepts.summary: Count elementary operations as a function of the problem size n and keep the dominant term: O(n²) versus O(n log n) decides what is feasible.
concepts.why: Exam questions often ask for the cost of an algorithm or how to reduce it.

concepts.title: Matrix products: views, cost and structure
concepts.summary: A matrix product can be read column-wise, row-wise or as a sum of outer products; it costs O(mnp), and structure (diagonal, triangular, blocks) can make it much cheaper.
concepts.why: Exploiting structure is the main source of speed in numpy code.

concepts.title: Low-rank products and evaluation order
concepts.summary: For A, B ∈ ℝ^{n×p} with p ≪ n, computing (ABᵀ)x as A(Bᵀx) costs O(np) instead of O(n²p).
concepts.why: Choosing the evaluation order turns infeasible computations into cheap ones.

concepts.title: Kronecker product
concepts.summary: A⊗B is the block matrix (a_ij B); (A⊗B)x can be computed by reshaping x into a matrix and doing two small products instead of forming A⊗B.
concepts.why: Tensor-product structure shows up in multi-dimensional quadrature and in exams.

concepts.title: The polynomial interpolation problem
concepts.summary: Given n+1 distinct nodes x_i with values y_i there is exactly one polynomial of degree ≤ n through them, because 𝒫ₙ has dimension n+1.
concepts.why: Interpolation is the building block for quadrature, differentiation and approximation.

concepts.title: Monomial basis, Vandermonde matrix and Horner
concepts.summary: Writing p in the monomial basis leads to a Vandermonde system (O(n³) and badly conditioned); Horner's scheme evaluates p(x) in O(n).
concepts.why: Shows why the choice of basis matters for cost and stability.

concepts.title: Newton basis
concepts.summary: The Newton basis N₀ = 1, N_j(x) = ∏_{k<j}(x − x_k) makes the interpolation system lower triangular, so adding a node adds only one new coefficient.
concepts.why: It makes interpolation incremental.

concepts.title: Divided differences and Newton's formula
concepts.summary: The Newton coefficients are the divided differences y[x₀,…,x_j], computed recursively in a triangular table in O(n²).
concepts.why: A classic exam computation, and the link to derivatives: y[x₀,…,xₙ] = f⁽ⁿ⁾(ξ)/n!.

concepts.title: Interpolation error formula
concepts.summary: f(x) − p(x) = f⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾(ξ)/(n+1)! · ∏(x − x_i): the smoothness of f and the node polynomial ∏(x − x_i) control the error.
concepts.why: This formula explains Runge's phenomenon and motivates Chebyshev nodes.

concepts.title: Lagrange polynomials
concepts.summary: ℓ_j(x) = ∏_{k≠j}(x − x_k)/(x_j − x_k) equals 1 at x_j and 0 at all other nodes, so p(x) = Σ y_j ℓ_j(x) needs no linear system.
concepts.why: A cardinal basis: the coefficients are the data values themselves.

concepts.title: Barycentric interpolation formula
concepts.summary: With weights λ_j = 1/∏_{k≠j}(x_j − x_k) precomputed in O(n²), p(x) = Σ λ_j y_j/(x − x_j) / Σ λ_j/(x − x_j) evaluates in O(n) and is numerically stable.
concepts.why: The practical way to evaluate polynomial interpolants.

concepts.title: Lebesgue constant and data errors
concepts.summary: Λₙ = max_x Σ|ℓ_j(x)| bounds how much errors in the data are amplified, ‖p − p̃‖_∞ ≤ Λₙ‖y − ỹ‖_∞; it depends only on the nodes.
concepts.why: Equispaced nodes have exponentially growing Λₙ, Chebyshev nodes only logarithmic growth.

concepts.title: Runge's phenomenon
concepts.summary: Interpolating 1/(1+25x²) at equispaced nodes diverges near the interval ends as n grows, although the function is perfectly smooth.
concepts.why: The cautionary tale that motivates choosing nodes carefully.

concepts.title: Chebyshev polynomials
concepts.summary: T_n(x) = cos(n arccos x) on [−1,1] with the recurrence T_{n+1} = 2xT_n − T_{n−1}; |T_n| ≤ 1, n zeros, n+1 extrema, leading coefficient 2ⁿ⁻¹.
concepts.why: Their zeros are the nodes that make the node polynomial as small as possible.

concepts.title: Chebyshev nodes and abscissae
concepts.summary: The zeros cos((2k+1)π/(2(n+1))) or the extrema cos(kπ/n) of the Chebyshev polynomials, mapped affinely to [a,b]; they cluster near the endpoints.
concepts.why: Clustering at the ends is exactly what suppresses Runge's oscillations.

concepts.title: Orthogonality of Chebyshev polynomials
concepts.summary: The T_n are orthogonal with respect to the weight 1/√(1−x²), and also discretely orthogonal on Chebyshev points.
concepts.why: Gives cheap formulas for Chebyshev coefficients and connects to Gauss quadrature.

concepts.title: Chebyshev interpolation error
concepts.summary: With Chebyshev nodes the node polynomial is 2⁻ⁿT_{n+1}, so ‖f − p‖_∞ ≤ ‖f⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾‖_∞/(2ⁿ(n+1)!), and Λₙ grows only like log n.
concepts.why: Explains why Chebyshev interpolation converges fast for smooth f.

concepts.title: Chebyshev expansion and Clenshaw's algorithm
concepts.summary: Write p = Σ c_k T_k with coefficients from discrete orthogonality, and evaluate it stably in O(n) with Clenshaw's backward recurrence.
concepts.why: The standard representation of interpolants in practice.

concepts.title: Trigonometric polynomials
concepts.summary: p(x) = Σ_{k=−m}^{m} c_k e^{2πikx} is 1-periodic; it is a polynomial in z = e^{2πix}.
concepts.why: The natural interpolant for periodic data.

concepts.title: L² inner product and the Fourier basis
concepts.summary: On L²(0,1) the inner product ⟨f,g⟩ = ∫₀¹ f ḡ dx makes φ_k(x) = e^{2πikx} an orthonormal system.
concepts.why: Orthonormality turns 'find the coefficients' into 'compute inner products'.

concepts.title: Fourier series and coefficients
concepts.summary: f̂(k) = ⟨f, φ_k⟩ = ∫₀¹ f(x) e^{−2πikx} dx and f = Σ f̂(k) φ_k in the L² sense; truncating gives the best L² approximation.
concepts.why: The continuous picture that the DFT approximates.

concepts.title: Parseval's identity and coefficient decay
concepts.summary: ‖f‖² = Σ|f̂(k)|²; differentiation multiplies f̂(k) by 2πik, so a smoother f has faster decaying coefficients (a jump gives decay like 1/k).
concepts.why: The decay rate predicts how well trigonometric approximation will work.

concepts.title: Roots of unity
concepts.summary: ω_N = e^{−2πi/N}; its powers lie on the unit circle and Σ_{j=0}^{N−1} ω_N^{jk} equals N if N divides k and 0 otherwise.
concepts.why: This sum identity is the reason the DFT basis is orthogonal.

concepts.title: Discrete Fourier transform and Fourier matrix
concepts.summary: Replacing the Fourier integral by the trapezoidal sum at N equispaced points gives the DFT with the Fourier matrix F_N = (ω_N^{jk}); F_N/√N is unitary, so the inverse is essentially the conjugate transpose.
concepts.why: Turns N samples into N frequency coefficients (and back) exactly.

concepts.title: numpy FFT conventions and fftshift
concepts.summary: np.fft.fft computes Σ y_j ω^{jk} without the factor 1/N, ifft includes 1/N; output index k ≥ N/2 stands for the negative frequency k − N, which fftshift moves to the front.
concepts.why: Most bugs in the exercises come from scaling and index ordering.

concepts.title: Frequency analysis, filtering and compression
concepts.summary: The power spectrum |c_k|² reveals dominant frequencies; zeroing small or high-frequency coefficients filters or compresses a signal.
concepts.why: The 'why care' of the DFT: EKG, MRI and vibration examples.

concepts.title: Circulant matrices and the convolution theorem
concepts.summary: Every circulant matrix is diagonalized by the Fourier matrix, so cyclic convolution becomes pointwise multiplication of DFTs: O(N log N) instead of O(N²).
concepts.why: Fast filtering and fast solution of circulant systems.

concepts.title: FFT: the fast Fourier transform
concepts.summary: Split the sum into even and odd indices: a DFT of length N becomes two DFTs of length N/2 plus O(N) work, giving O(N log N) overall.
concepts.why: Makes everything in this chapter practical.

concepts.title: Trigonometric interpolation via the DFT
concepts.summary: Sample f at n equispaced points, get the coefficients with one FFT, then evaluate the trigonometric interpolant anywhere. The sampling grid (n points) and the evaluation grid (N points) are different things.
concepts.why: Core exam topic, and it separates 'coefficients' from 'values'.

concepts.title: Evaluation by zero-padding
concepts.summary: To evaluate the interpolant on a finer equispaced grid of N > n points, pad the (shifted) coefficient vector with zeros to length N and apply one inverse FFT.
concepts.why: Efficient O(N log N) evaluation; the trick behind evaliptrig.

concepts.title: Aliasing
concepts.summary: On n samples the frequencies k and k + n are indistinguishable, so each discrete coefficient is the sum of the true coefficients f̂(k + ℓn).
concepts.why: Explains interpolation errors and the sampling theorem.

concepts.title: Trigonometric interpolation error and the sampling theorem
concepts.summary: The error is controlled by the tail Σ_{|k|>n/2} |f̂(k)|: algebraic decay for C^p functions, exponential for analytic ones, and band-limited f is reproduced exactly.
concepts.why: Lets you predict convergence rates from smoothness, a typical exam question.

concepts.title: Chebyshev interpolation with the DFT
concepts.summary: With x = cos θ, Chebyshev interpolation becomes cosine interpolation in θ, so the Chebyshev coefficients can be computed with an FFT in O(n log n).
concepts.why: Links chapters 2 and 3 and is used by Clenshaw–Curtis quadrature.

concepts.title: Piecewise linear interpolation
concepts.summary: Connect neighbouring data points by straight lines: local, shape-preserving, with error O(h²)·max|f''|.
concepts.why: Avoids the global wiggles of high-degree polynomials.

concepts.title: Cubic Hermite interpolation
concepts.summary: On each interval use the cubic that matches values and slopes at both ends; the result is C¹ with error O(h⁴) if the slopes are exact.
concepts.why: Gives smooth curves when derivatives are known or can be estimated.

concepts.title: Cubic splines
concepts.summary: Piecewise cubics that are C² at the knots; the two missing conditions come from complete, natural, periodic or not-a-knot end conditions, which leads to a tridiagonal system.
concepts.why: The default smooth interpolant in practice (scipy CubicSpline).

concepts.title: Spline error and minimal curvature
concepts.summary: Complete cubic splines have error O(h⁴); the natural spline minimizes ∫(s'')² among all C² interpolants.
concepts.why: Explains why splines look 'natural'.

concepts.title: Quadrature rules: nodes, weights, error
concepts.summary: Approximate ∫_a^b f(x) dx by Σ w_i f(c_i); the quadrature error depends on the rule and on the smoothness of f.
concepts.why: Most integrals in practice have no closed form.

concepts.title: Interpolatory quadrature
concepts.summary: Integrate the interpolation polynomial instead of f: w_i = ∫ ℓ_i(x) dx, so the rule is exact for polynomials of degree ≤ n.
concepts.why: Connects chapter 2 to quadrature.

concepts.title: Order of a quadrature rule
concepts.summary: Order s means the rule is exact for all polynomials of degree ≤ s − 1; symmetric rules have even order; rules are transformed affinely to [−1,1].
concepts.why: The order determines the convergence rate of composite rules.

concepts.title: Midpoint, trapezoidal and Simpson rules
concepts.summary: Equispaced interpolatory rules with orders 2, 2 and 4 and error constants obtained from Taylor expansions.
concepts.why: The workhorse rules you must be able to derive and apply.

concepts.title: Composite rules and convergence
concepts.summary: Split [a,b] into N subintervals of width h and apply a rule of order s on each: the error is O(h^s) = O(N^{−s}), a line of slope −s in a log-log plot.
concepts.why: How you read convergence plots in exercises and exams.

concepts.title: Trapezoidal rule for periodic functions
concepts.summary: For smooth periodic integrands the composite trapezoidal rule converges exponentially, because it integrates e^{2πikx} exactly for |k| < N.
concepts.why: Surprising 'free' accuracy that links quadrature and the DFT.

concepts.title: Romberg integration
concepts.summary: The trapezoidal error expands in even powers of h; Richardson extrapolation on successive halvings removes these terms one by one.
concepts.why: High order from a very simple rule.

concepts.title: Gauss quadrature
concepts.summary: With s nodes the maximal order is 2s, reached exactly when the nodes are the zeros of the degree-s orthogonal polynomial (Legendre for weight 1).
concepts.why: The best accuracy per function evaluation.

concepts.title: Gauss–Legendre nodes, weights and error
concepts.summary: The nodes are Legendre zeros, the weights are positive (hence stable) and follow from integrals of Lagrange polynomials; the error scales with f^{(2s)}.
concepts.why: What scipy's fixed_quad does; positivity explains its stability.

concepts.title: Clenshaw–Curtis quadrature
concepts.summary: Interpolate at Chebyshev points and integrate the Chebyshev expansion exactly; weights come from an FFT, nodes are nested, and accuracy is close to Gauss.
concepts.why: A practical alternative to Gauss with cheap weights.

concepts.title: Adaptive quadrature
concepts.summary: Estimate the local error on each subinterval by comparing two rules, and refine only where the estimate is large.
concepts.why: Efficient for integrands whose difficulty is localized.

concepts.title: Quadrature in higher dimensions and sparse grids
concepts.summary: Tensor-product rules need N^d points (curse of dimensionality); sparse grids combine coarse tensor rules to cut this drastically for smooth integrands.
concepts.why: Why high-dimensional integration needs different ideas.

concepts.title: Monte Carlo quadrature
concepts.summary: Estimate ∫f as the mean of f at random points: the error behaves like σ/√N independent of the dimension, with confidence intervals from the central limit theorem.
concepts.why: The only practical approach in very high dimensions.

concepts.title: Variance reduction
concepts.summary: Since the error is σ/√N, reduce σ: importance sampling, control variates and antithetic variables.
concepts.why: The same accuracy with far fewer samples.

concepts.title: Iterative methods and convergence order
concepts.summary: An iteration produces x⁽ᵏ⁾ → x*; order p means ‖e_{k+1}‖ ≈ C‖e_k‖ᵖ: linear convergence is a straight line in a lin-log plot, quadratic convergence doubles the correct digits.
concepts.why: Reading convergence from error tables and plots is a standard exam task.

concepts.title: Stopping criteria
concepts.summary: Stop on a small residual, a small correction, or the a-posteriori bound ‖x⁽ᵏ⁾ − x*‖ ≤ L/(1−L)·‖x⁽ᵏ⁾ − x⁽ᵏ⁻¹⁾‖ for linear convergence.
concepts.why: A small correction does not always mean a small error.

concepts.title: Fixed-point iteration and contraction
concepts.summary: Rewrite F(x) = 0 as x = Φ(x) and iterate. If Φ is a contraction near x* (|Φ'| ≤ L < 1) it converges linearly with rate L; Φ'(x*) = 0 gives higher order.
concepts.why: The unifying theory behind Newton's method and its relatives.

concepts.title: Bisection
concepts.summary: If f changes sign on [a,b], halving the interval keeps a root inside: robust, with linear convergence of rate 1/2.
concepts.why: Guaranteed but slow, which makes it a good safeguard.

concepts.title: Newton's method in 1D
concepts.summary: x_{k+1} = x_k − f(x_k)/f'(x_k) linearizes f at x_k; it converges quadratically near simple roots and only linearly near multiple roots.
concepts.why: The most important root-finding method.

concepts.title: Secant method
concepts.summary: Replace f' by the slope through the last two iterates: no derivatives needed, convergence order (1+√5)/2 ≈ 1.618.
concepts.why: Often more efficient per function evaluation than Newton.

concepts.title: Newton's method in d dimensions
concepts.summary: Solve the linear system DF(x_k) s = −F(x_k) with the Jacobian and set x_{k+1} = x_k + s; simplified Newton reuses an old Jacobian and its LU factors.
concepts.why: Nonlinear systems are everywhere, including least squares.

concepts.title: Damped Newton
concepts.summary: Take x_{k+1} = x_k + λ_k s_k with a step length λ_k chosen by a monotonicity test to enlarge the region of convergence.
concepts.why: Reduces Newton's dependence on a good starting value, though not always.

concepts.title: Quasi-Newton (Broyden) method
concepts.summary: Avoid recomputing Jacobians by updating an approximation J_k with a rank-1 correction that satisfies the secant condition.
concepts.why: Cheap iterations for large systems, built on low-rank tricks.

concepts.title: Orthogonal and unitary matrices
concepts.summary: QᴴQ = I: the columns are orthonormal, ‖Qx‖ = ‖x‖ and Q⁻¹ = Qᴴ; rotations and permutations are examples.
concepts.why: Transformations that never amplify errors.

concepts.title: Gram–Schmidt and the QR decomposition
concepts.summary: Orthonormalizing the columns of A one after another gives A = QR with R upper triangular.
concepts.why: The conceptual route to QR (numerically you use Householder).

concepts.title: Gaussian elimination and LU decomposition
concepts.summary: Elimination factors PA = LU in O(n³); afterwards each solve is just two triangular solves in O(n²).
concepts.why: Factor once, solve many times: a key to efficient code.

concepts.title: Matrix norms and the condition number
concepts.summary: cond(A) = ‖A‖‖A⁻¹‖ bounds how relative errors in b are amplified in the solution x; orthogonal transformations leave it unchanged.
concepts.why: Explains when a linear system cannot be solved accurately.

concepts.title: Householder and Givens QR
concepts.summary: Reflections or rotations zero out entries column by column and give a stable QR decomposition in O(mn²).
concepts.why: The stable way to orthogonalize, used for least squares.

concepts.title: Singular value decomposition
concepts.summary: Every matrix factors as A = UΣVᴴ with unitary U, V and σ₁ ≥ σ₂ ≥ … ≥ 0: A maps the right singular vectors to σ_i times the left ones.
concepts.why: The master decomposition for rank, norms, low-rank approximation and PCA.

concepts.title: Rank, norms and condition via the SVD
concepts.summary: The rank is the number of nonzero σ_i, ‖A‖₂ = σ₁, cond₂(A) = σ₁/σₙ and ‖A‖_F² = Σσ_i²; numerical rank uses a tolerance.
concepts.why: Reading matrix properties directly from the singular values.

concepts.title: Best low-rank approximation and PCA
concepts.summary: Truncating the SVD after k terms gives the best rank-k approximation in the 2- and Frobenius norm; PCA finds the dominant directions in data.
concepts.why: Compression and data analysis.

concepts.title: Linear least squares
concepts.summary: For an overdetermined system Ax ≈ b, find the x that minimizes ‖b − Ax‖₂; fitting a model that is linear in its parameters is the typical case.
concepts.why: Measurements are noisy and plentiful, so exact solutions do not exist.

concepts.title: Normal equations
concepts.summary: The minimizer satisfies AᴴAx = Aᴴb (the residual is orthogonal to the range of A); cheap, but it squares the condition number.
concepts.why: Simple to derive, and a classic stability pitfall.

concepts.title: Least squares via QR
concepts.summary: With A = QR, ‖b − Ax‖ = ‖Qᴴb − Rx‖, so you solve the triangular system R₁x = (Qᴴb)₁; stable because the condition number is not squared.
concepts.why: The recommended method in practice.

concepts.title: Least squares via SVD and the pseudoinverse
concepts.summary: x = VΣ⁺Uᴴb is the minimal-norm least squares solution, also when A is rank-deficient.
concepts.why: Handles rank deficiency and regularization.

concepts.title: Total least squares
concepts.summary: When A is noisy too, find the smallest perturbation of [A b] that makes the system consistent; the solution comes from the last right singular vector.
concepts.why: Fitting when both variables carry errors.

concepts.title: Nonlinear least squares
concepts.summary: Minimize ‖F(x)‖² for a model that is nonlinear in its parameters; Newton's method on the gradient needs second derivatives.
concepts.why: Real models (exponentials, GPS) are nonlinear in the parameters.

concepts.title: Gauss–Newton method
concepts.summary: Linearize F at x_k and solve a linear least squares problem for the step: no second derivatives, and fast near a good fit.
concepts.why: The standard method for nonlinear fitting.

concepts.title: BFGS, gradient descent, SGD, CG, Levenberg–Marquardt, Adam
concepts.de: Weitere Methoden: BFGS, GD, SGD, CG, LM, ADAM
concepts.summary: Trade-offs between cost per step and convergence: GD and SGD use only gradients, LM blends GD and Gauss–Newton, BFGS builds curvature from updates, Adam adapts step sizes.
concepts.why: The bridge from numerics to training neural networks.

concepts.title: Neural networks and backpropagation
concepts.summary: A DNN composes affine maps and nonlinearities and is fitted by (stochastic) least squares; backpropagation computes the gradient with the chain rule in reverse.
concepts.why: Shows modern ML as a nonlinear least squares problem.

concepts.title: Physics-informed neural networks
concepts.summary: Add the residual of a differential equation to the loss so that the network fits data and physics at the same time.
concepts.why: A current research application of the chapter.
